summary.text: A 79-year-old Caucasian female with coronary artery disease, severe aortic stenosis, essential hypertension, dyslipidemia and a prior angioplasty presented to the emergency department with seven hours of persistent shortness of breath and rapid irregular palpitations. Initial blood pressure was 71/50 mmHg and rose to 107/61 mmHg within five minutes. Electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and chest X-ray showed increased pulmonary vasculature markings.

Intravenous heparin was started and urgent electrical cardioversion, given the clinical picture of pulmonary edema, restored sinus rhythm. Echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular function, moderate left ventricular hypertrophy, a severely dilated left atrium, and severe aortic and moderate mitral valve stenosis. Oral amiodarone loading of 400 mg three times per day began on the first day of admission.

On the fourth day following admission she developed mild shortness of breath. Separately, her sodium was noted to have dropped from 134 meq/l to 126 meq/l (the day of this first drop is not stated in the case text); furosemide was given, hydrochlorothiazide was resumed, and amiodarone was reduced. On the sixth day she had nausea, generalized weakness, headache and blurred vision, and sodium continued to fall to 113 meq/l on the seventh day with a nadir of 110 meq/l. SIADH was suspected, and acute kidney injury, hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency were ruled out.

Fluid restriction and tolvaptan were given, followed by dextrose 5% water and desmopressin after sodium rose by 15 meq/l in 24 hours, and sodium then dropped to 120 meq/l on day 10. Amiodarone was discontinued on the ninth day, sotalol was started 48 hours later and sodium chloride tablets were added; sodium improved to 129 meq/l on day 13 and 135 meq/l on day 18.
